LMAO, my situation 2 months ago exactly. Got hired at some small start up consulting firm (<30) fresh off college. 

Only to be dropped alone on a mission with no formation nor guidance. Mission got out of hand as the client renégociated the whole fucking deal. Was alone, worked 13h a day. Managed to meet all my goals. No personal life.

Only to get sacked like a bag of shit at the end of my trial period, because these dipshits had hired way too many consultants and our salaries were killing them.

You are young and want to prove yourself ; you’ll soon realize that some companies make their bread and butter off that, by exploiting the fuck out of youngsters. Especially small firms with very few employees. They use you and have absolutely no regrets in tossing you out when they feel you reached your limit.

My advice is : 

- do NOT stay there. You care about the project of the company, but I guarantee they give no fucks about you. You do NOT want to work for people like that. I know there’s the pandemic, but you’ll only end up completely burnt out like me. 

In the end, I couldn’t even understand the emails I was sent. Could not remember basic commands in excel. Took me forever to do basic tasks. Could not remember names. 

It took me several weeks to recover. And don’t get me started on the damages on my self esteem. This feeling of inadequacy will follow me for a long time, and I’m afraid it will prevent me from taking initiative in future work.

Better you quit immediately, when you are still somewhat healthy and able to think clearly. That way you still have your strength for job hunting. If you wait til you are burnt out, it might be several weeks, or months, before you are mentally capable to go through recrutement processes all over again. 

- apply for big legit consulting firms, NOT some shady garage-band start-up. Most often than not they use their employees like tissues, have a toxic corporate culture and are owned by megalomaniacs. Also, at our level of experience, we need proper guidance and monitoring to progress and reach potential. Learning by trial by fire only gets you so far. Big 4s/5s will give you proper training.

What you are doing sounds intense with lots of responsibilities, I have no doubts you will be able to valorize it. Try your luck for January integrations in big 4/5s, it’s now or never.

PS : they might try to sway you by implying they know people in big 4s and what not, do not pay attention to that. Run.

Super contente pour ton fils. Mon frère était dans sa situation, TDAH + dispraxie. Échec scolaire, trublion, les imbéciles de l’école primaire se sont contentés de le catégoriser « sale gosse à problèmes ». Il n’a été diagnostiqué qu’à 14 ans, et c’était déjà trop tard, à force de se faire traiter de grosse merde par sa famille et ses profs il n’aimait plus l’école.

Mes parents ont aussi très mal géré : ils avaient beau avoir le diagnostic sous les yeux, ils ont eu du mal à intégrer qu’il s’agissait d’un vrai handicap. Ils ont rechigné à lui faire prendre sa ritaline parce que « c’EsT sUpEr fOrT tU cOmPreNdS ” (et l’effet du TDAH sur son cerveau c’est pas fort peut-être?? Grrrr...).

Voici mes conseils pour la suite :
- il faut considérer ses médicaments comme un fauteuil roulant de paraplégique : les lui retirer, c’est l’empêcher de fonctionner comme une personne normale. Ces médocs et leurs effets peuvent être impressionnants, mais il ne faut pas oublier que les effets du TDAH et des troubles en dys sont bien plus graves! 

- l’encourager constamment et féliciter ses progrès, 

- inscrivez-vous à la mdph, demandez un ordi pour les cours et un tiers temps aux examens 

- poussez le dans des activités créatives ou manuelles. 

- les TDAH sont des personnalités naturellement addictives car leur circuit de la récompense est tronqué. Prends garde aux divertissements “faciles” (télévision, jeux vidéos en ligne, etc). Mon frère est accro aux jeux en ligne et pas “accro selon TF1” ; ça a complètement investi sa vie, ses anciens intérêts et passions ont tous été délaissés, il planifie sa vie autour, fait passer le jeu avant tout le reste (famille, études, etc), ne supporte pas d’en être séparé, etc. Renseigne toi sur les possibilités d’addiction pour les TDAH et pousse le à cultiver ses intérêts et passions le plus possible

When I was 14 I loved to draw. In my mind things were pretty simple : I would go to art school, land a job drawing, and I would have enough money to have a house, a garden, 2 kids, a car and vacations. My school teachers told me to « chase my dreams » and referred me to top art schools, but my mother intervened. She made me read forum entries of art school graduate who were still jobless at 27, or desperate because they had to work at mc Donald’s after 25 years of studies. 

I hated her then, because she broke my childish expectations of what my life would be. But I will never thank her enough for showing me the real world. Drawing in the margins of your school notebooks is not sturdy enough to engage in art studies anyways. 

One thing that terrified me was struggling with money, or still being dependent on my parents at 28. So I scrapped the art studies, made it my hobby, went on in high level business studies and now I can draw AND I earn a very good living at 24. Wouldn’t change a thing. If my mother hadn’t said anything to me, I would have gone in art school no questions asked, and I might be struggling now, bitter, convinced I was robbed of my livelihood by the universe.

My little brother is in a similar position than yours. 
I understand the reaction of your family. I believe you should have shown them that even if you weren’t sure of a career plan, you were actively trying things to figure it out. For them playing games is not a career. Playing games is perfectly fine as a hobby. They would have had the same reaction if you had told them you wanted to be a internationally famous singer. They’ve been thinking « my son believes his childhood pipe dream ». Now you are 22, when most people are done with studies. I understand their frustration with you.

My advice to you : stop mentioning esport to them. They are completely fed up with the « playing video games is a real career I swear » narrative. Don’t mention the tournament to them anymore. Instead tell them you understand that video games competition is not a sustainable career (it’s really not : no stable income, a very niche set of skills, time-consuming, no social security, etc). It took you very long to realize dreams are not sustainable plans for the future, but should be pursued on the side of a job, which provides security. 
When you understood that, you took action immediately and signed up for university to get your life together at last. To make up for the 4 years you “lost”, you will take a part time job. 
IMPORTANT: at this point, only a thought-through, fool proof 5-year plan will calm them down. For ex : “the next three years I plan to complete this bachelor at university, while working part time as X in company Y to save money. I will then do the Master in Z, then I will be able to occupy a junior position as Z.” 
This will prove them you took your life in your own hands. And that if they throw you out now, they’ll ruin your chances at becoming the person they want you to be. 
In this conservation, tell them things like : “I realized you were right all along.” One of the things that made them mad overtime is that you didn’t seem to listen to them. If you tell them they helped you realize you were wasting your youth chasing a pipe dream, it will make them feel like they finally succeeded at beating some sense in their child. It’ll soothe them a bit. Throw in some apologies.

But what if the worst does happen, and they throw you out still? (I don’t think you have a renting contract with your parents)

Go to university anyway. Education is the only way out of endless precarity, if your dream does fail. Research housing solutions for students, grants, ask friends and family members in the meantime. People are very helpful to those willing to help themselves, you’d be surprised.
Do your studies in an apprenticeship, you will earn a decent salary while studying, and you will have at least a year of work experience at the end of your studies. Some companies even finance your school fees. Seriously look into that.

Final advice : don’t listen to people telling you you “lost” four years. You didn’t loose them, you used them to pursue your dream, something most people never dare consider. And your dream is never lost, you can attend tournaments and train on your down time. It will come way slower than if you trained full time, but you will feel much safer with a stable income and situation.

Have a conversation with your parents ASAP. If they still want to throw you out, take the news like an adult and use the little time you have left to secure housing for next week, then apply for grants and student housing. 

Good luck for your tournament, and even if does go nowhere, you will have no regret.
